passage: The tennis ball flew off Mohit's bat and cracked the glass pane of Ramdin kaka's cycle-repair shop near the bus stand. The whole pane fell in pieces. Mohit's elder sister Sudha grabbed his arm. "Now what? You'll have to tell Kaka." Mohit pulled free. "It's just one small glass. Last Diwali the big boys burst crackers inside his shed and burned the tyres. That was much worse, and nobody even caught them!" "So?" said Sudha. "His glass is still broken." Mohit scuffed his chappal in the dust and looked toward the shop, where Kaka was already sweeping up the pieces with a bent broom.

qa.q: What did Mohit's tennis ball break?
qa.a: It cracked the glass pane of Ramdin kaka's cycle-repair shop near the bus stand.

qa.q: Why did it feel reasonable to Mohit to call it just one small glass?
qa.a: Next to the big boys burning Kaka's tyres last Diwali, one pane seems tiny to him, so he feels he hasn't done anything serious.

qa.q: What could Mohit do right now, while Kaka is sweeping?
qa.a: He could walk over with Sudha, say the ball was his, apologise and ask how he can help fix it.

qa.q: How does the broken glass look from Ramdin kaka's side?
qa.a: For Kaka it is his shop window and his mess to sweep up; it hardly matters to him that other boys once did worse.

grounding: A village boy shrinks the window he broke by pointing to the older boys' worse damage.

passage: Snow still lay along the fence on Ingrid's street in Bergen when her kick sent the football straight through Mr Olsen's garage window. Rafael, her friend from next door, gasped. "He's going to be so mad." Ingrid crossed her arms. "It's one window. Remember when the teenagers spray-painted the whole bus shelter? And they smashed the lamp at the park. This is nothing next to that." Rafael looked at the jagged hole. "But we did this one." Ingrid didn't answer. She kept her hands in her jacket pockets, and when the garage door creaked open, she took a small step back behind Rafael.

qa.q: What had the teenagers done that Ingrid brought up?
qa.a: They spray-painted the whole bus shelter and smashed the lamp at the park.

qa.q: What does Ingrid's step back behind Rafael suggest about how she really feels?
qa.a: Even while calling it nothing, she seems nervous and a bit guilty, which hints she knows the window still matters 😰.

qa.q: What choice could Ingrid make when the garage door opens?
qa.a: She could step forward, tell Mr Olsen the kick was hers, apologise, and offer to help sort out the window.

qa.q: How does Rafael see the window differently from Ingrid?
qa.a: Rafael doesn't compare it with the teenagers at all; Rafael looks at the hole and sees that they did this one.

grounding: A girl in Norway calls the window she broke nothing next to what the teenagers did.

subtype: At least it was not worse [Actor]
passage: In the boys' hostel common room, Madhav was bouncing a rubber ball off the wall during study hour. One bounce went wide and cracked the window beside the notice board. Shankar sir, the warden, came in holding his register. "Who did this?" Madhav raised his hand slowly, then added quickly, "Sir, it's just a crack. Last term the Class 8 boys broke three whole bulbs and the fan regulator. This is nothing compared to that." Shankar sir looked at the crack, then at him. "Were you in Class 8 last term?" "No, sir." "Then let's talk about this window." Madhav's ears went red. He picked up the ball and held it behind his back.

qa.q: What cracked the window in the common room?
qa.a: One bounce of Madhav's rubber ball went wide and cracked the window beside the notice board.

qa.q: Why did Madhav quickly bring up the Class 8 boys?
qa.a: Pointing to three bulbs and a fan regulator made his crack seem tiny, so he could feel less guilty and hope for less trouble.

qa.q: What could Madhav say next that would help put things right?
qa.a: He could say, "I cracked it during study hour, I'm sorry," and ask what he can do to help get it repaired.

qa.q: How might Shankar sir see Madhav's comparison?
qa.a: The warden seems to see it as a way of dodging, so he gently brings the talk back to this one window and Madhav's part in it.

grounding: A hostel boy tries to make a cracked window look small by comparing it with the older boys' damage.

passage:
I'm Baljeet. I sit next to Lokesh in Class 4. On Friday, while we waited for the bell, Lokesh threw his steel water bottle up to catch it, showing off. It went sideways and cracked the staffroom window. A long line ran right across the glass.
Ma'am asked who did it. Lokesh put his hand up slowly, but then he said, 'It's only a crack. Last year the Class 7 boys broke three windows and the fan.'
Ma'am said, 'We're talking about this window.'
Lokesh kept saying 'only a crack' all through lunch. But he didn't eat his paratha, and he kept looking at the staffroom. I don't know what he was thinking. Maybe he was scared of his papa finding out.

qa.q: What did Lokesh throw that cracked the staffroom window?
qa.a: His steel water bottle.

qa.q: Why did comparing with the Class 7 boys feel reasonable to Lokesh?
qa.a: Next to three windows and a fan, one crack seemed small; the comparison made Lokesh's own damage feel less serious and less scary.

qa.q: What choice could Lokesh make instead of saying 'only a crack'?
qa.a: Lokesh could say 'I broke it, sorry' and offer to help set it right; owning this crack without comparing it to anyone else might also ease the worry.

qa.q: How does Baljeet read Lokesh's 'only a crack' alongside the uneaten paratha?
qa.a: Baljeet notices the words and the behaviour don't match: Lokesh insists it is small but skips lunch and keeps looking at the staffroom, so Baljeet guesses at fear without being sure.

grounding: A classmate watches a child who cracked a window say it is nothing compared with what older boys broke, shrinking his own act by comparison.

passage:
Saturday: Parveen was pulling in her kite on the terrace when her foot knocked a flowerpot off the ledge. It smashed the window of the flat below, where Ujjwal bhaiya lived. Parveen hid behind the water tank.
Sunday: Ujjwal bhaiya knocked on their door holding the broken pot. Parveen's words came out fast. 'It's just one window! Last Diwali the building boys burst crackers in his letterbox. That was much worse!'
Ammi said quietly, 'Is that the same thing?'
Wednesday: Parveen went downstairs with her piggy bank and a card. 'Sorry I broke your window, bhaiya. And sorry I talked about the boys.' Ujjwal bhaiya smiled, kept the card, and gave back the piggy bank. 'Help me water my plants this week instead.'

qa.q: What knocked the flowerpot off the ledge?
qa.a: Parveen's foot, while she was pulling in her kite on the terrace.

qa.q: Why did Parveen bring up the Diwali crackers on Sunday?
qa.a: Parveen was scared of getting into trouble, and comparing with something worse made one broken window feel small and less her fault.

qa.q: What was the turning point for Parveen, and what did she choose to do?
qa.a: Ammi's quiet question, 'Is that the same thing?'; on Wednesday Parveen went down with her piggy bank and a card and apologised for the window and for the comparison.

qa.q: How might Ujjwal bhaiya have felt hearing about the Diwali crackers instead of an apology?
qa.a: He probably felt his broken window was being brushed aside; the Wednesday apology let him feel heard, so he offered plant watering instead of taking money.

grounding: A child who broke a neighbour's window says it is just one window compared with older boys' pranks, then owns it after being asked if it is the same.
